Fratricide means the killing of one's own brother. That's the single clearest, most direct definition. Everything else about this word grows outward from that center.
Two Things the Word Can Mean at Once

This is important: the same word, fratricide, can refer to two different things depending on how it's used in a sentence.

1. The act itself
The killing of one's own brother is called a fratricide.

"The king's rise to power involved fratricide — he had his own brother murdered."

2. The person who commits the act
A person who kills their own brother is also called a fratricide.

"He was known throughout the kingdom as a fratricide."

So the word can name both the deed and the doer. Context will always make clear which one is meant.
Does It Only Apply to Brothers?

Strictly speaking, yes — the word literally refers to a brother. The precise technical term for killing a sister is sororicide. However, in modern usage, you will sometimes see fratricide used more loosely to include the killing of a sister as well, particularly when the emphasis is on the closeness of the family bond rather than the gender. In formal, precise writing, though, it refers specifically to a brother.

In military and defense contexts, fratricide takes on a very specific and important meaning: the accidental killing of one's own soldiers or allies during combat.

This is sometimes called "friendly fire," but fratricide specifically refers to cases where that friendly fire results in death. It's one of the most painful and demoralizing things that can happen in warfare — soldiers losing their lives not to the enemy, but to their own side's weapons, bombs, or mistakes.

"The investigation revealed that the soldiers had died from fratricide — a missile fired by their own aircraft."

Militaries around the world spend enormous resources on training, communication systems, and technology specifically designed to prevent fratricide.

Beyond its literal and military meanings, fratricide is also used figuratively — to describe situations where members of the same group, team, or side turn on and destroy each other, ultimately weakening or ruining the whole group.

This usage is especially common in politics.

"The two candidates from the same party attacked each other so viciously during the primaries that political analysts called it fratricide — by the time the general election arrived, both their reputations were in ruins."

The logic is the same as the literal meaning: instead of fighting the real opponent, you are destroying someone on your own side.
Famous Examples to Make It Stick

Real and mythological examples help cement the meaning deeply.

Cain and Abel (The Bible): This is the most universally known act of fratricide in human culture. Cain, out of jealousy, kills his brother Abel. It is so iconic that fratricide is sometimes simply called "the sin of Cain."

Romulus and Remus (Roman Mythology): The twin brothers who, according to legend, founded Rome. Romulus killed Remus in a dispute, making the very founding of Rome an act of fratricide.

Ottoman Empire (History): For centuries, it was an actual legal and accepted practice for a new Ottoman sultan to have all of his brothers executed upon taking the throne — to eliminate rivals. This institutionalized fratricide was codified in law.

It's worth understanding why this word exists as its own distinct term, rather than just saying "he killed his brother." The reason is moral weight. Killing a brother is considered one of the deepest possible betrayals — a violation of the most fundamental bond of loyalty, family, and shared blood. The word fratricide captures not just the act of killing, but the profound wrongness and tragedy of who was killed and by whom. It carries a sense of horror and betrayal that a plain phrase like "killed his brother" does not fully convey.

This is also why the word transfers so powerfully to the figurative uses — whether in war or politics, the idea being conveyed is always: you have destroyed someone who was supposed to be on your side, someone close to you, someone who trusted you.
